insider_note: The counts are twenty six-membered and twelve five-membered rings, and the number sixty is the count of carbon atoms, not of rings.

steps.label: The two counts
lines: That is thirty-two rings in all.
The sixty carbon atoms of the molecule

steps.why: The question asks for two numbers, so both are named separately: twelve rings of five carbon atoms and twenty rings of six. Together those thirty-two rings close the cage that carries the sixty carbon atoms.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two numbers. There are twelve five-membered rings and twenty six-membered rings.
Writing sixty as a ring count. Sixty is the number of carbon atoms in C₆₀, not the number of rings.
steps.memory_tip: Twelve five-membered rings and twenty six-membered rings, thirty-two rings in all.
steps.margin_note: Write both counts on one line, each with its ring size named next to it.

steps.why: The two counts say how many rings there are but not how they are placed. The fusion rule adds that: every five-membered ring is surrounded by six-membered rings, so the twelve of them are spread over the cage rather than joined together.
common_mistakes: Writing that two five-membered rings are fused to each other. A five-membered ring is fused only to six-membered rings.
Writing that a six-membered ring is fused only to six-membered rings. It may also be fused to a five-membered ring.
steps.memory_tip: Five-membered rings are never fused to each other; each one is surrounded by six-membered rings.
steps.margin_note: One line naming the fusion rule completes the answer after the two counts.
